ranked.title: Agent overwrites its sole control-plane trust anchor with the ca_pem of an unauthenticated re-key response, over a channel that ships as plain HTTP
ranked.failure_sequence:
UNVERIFIED — raised by the completeness critic; no adversarial lens ran on it. Eight finders checked what the CP accepts; none checked what the agent accepts back.

State: a gateway on the shipped default. main.go:42 `apiURL := getenv("TUNNEX_API_URL", "http://api:8080")` — plain HTTP, and that literal is what docker-compose.yml:89, deploy/tunnex.yml:89 and .env.example:27 set; the S8.2c cross-cloud walk ran a real gateway with TUNNEX_API_URL="http://40.65.63.141" over the public internet (walk-artifacts/S8.2c/walk-record.md:22). Both re-key round trips go over apiURL (control/rekey.go:183, :208), NOT over the CA-pinned mTLS channel at agentURL.

1. Force the path: blackhole the gateway's 8443 traffic for 48h so renewal cannot run and the cert expires, or simply wait for the case the code itself names, "a gateway rebooting after a weekend" (main.go:776). On restart identity.Decide returns Recover from the agent's own clock with no network call, and attemptRekey runs (main.go:77).
2. Answer as the server from any on-path position for that http:// URL (ARP/DNS spoof on the LAN, a rogue pod answering the `api` Service name, a hop on the public path): reply 200 {"nonce":"<any 32 bytes>"} — rekeyChallenge (control/rekey.go:206-228) validates nothing about the server. The agent signs (nonce ‖ CSR DER) and submits. Reply 200 with cert_pem = a cert for CN=nodeName signed by the ATTACKER's CA and ca_pem = the attacker's CA. control.Rekey (rekey.go:193-203) checks only StatusCode == 200 and returns both blobs verbatim.
3. main.go:861 calls saveCreds(certDir, newCert, pending, newCA). saveCreds (main.go:441) writes ca.pem, cert.pem, key.pem unconditionally — no parse, no chain check, no check that newCert's public key is the pending key, no comparison against the CA already on disk. main.go:454 then deletes the pending key, destroying the remaining recovery material.
4. ca.pem is the ONLY RootCAs for the control channel (control/client.go:94-106 AppendCertsFromPEM / RootCAs: pool; main.go:152 builds the client from the bytes re-key just returned). The gateway now trusts the attacker's CA as its control plane and presents an attacker-issued client cert to it; the same on-path attacker terminates agentURL and pushes arbitrary peers, AllowedIPs, policy artifacts, routed ranges, site links and DNS forwarding as desired state.

Smoking gun: caPEM — the anchor the agent has pinned since enrolment — is passed INTO attemptRekey (main.go:791) and referenced nowhere in the body. Contrast renewLoop, the steady-state path, which deliberately re-reads the on-disk anchor (main.go:509) and writes it back unchanged.
ranked.why_it_matters: If it holds, this is the only place in the product where an unauthenticated network peer can replace a gateway's cryptographic trust anchor, and S13.1 made it reachable with no human action — converting a transient on-path position plus 48h of denied connectivity into permanent control-plane impersonation. Every downstream control (policy compilation, grants, kill-switches) derives from desired state the attacker then supplies, so the CP-side gone-gate, PoP and uniform refusal are all irrelevant. docs/S13.1-decisions.md never mentions ca_pem, the trust anchor, or agent-side response validation — the property was never stated, so nothing checked it. It must be verified before anything else on this list is dispositioned.
ranked.suggested_direction: Verify first, then rule. Never write ca_pem from the re-key response — mirror renewLoop and keep the on-disk anchor (already passed in at main.go:791). Before promoting, require the returned cert to parse, chain to the existing ca.pem, and bind the pending public key; refuse and retry otherwise, leaving the pending key intact. If CA rotation must ride this path, require cross-signing by the current CA. Red: feed attemptRekey a hostile server (attacker CA + mismatched cert) and assert ca.pem/cert.pem/key.pem unchanged and the pending key surviving.

ranked.title: nodes.Revoke cascades across tenants: the node is never resolved inside the org, RevokeNode is :exec so the mismatch is silent, and the device/OVPN sweeps are keyed on node_id alone
ranked.failure_sequence:
Two finders (gate, sql) found this independently; all four verdicts confirmed it.

State: Mallory is owner of org A (self-signup, so PermOrgUpdate is free) and a plain member of org B. Org B has gateway node N, whose UUID any member can read (ListNodes gates on PermOrgView; S8.3 gave members org:view over the topology).

1. Mallory POSTs /api/v1/organizations/{A}/nodes/{N}/revoke. node_handlers.go:112 runs authorize(ctx, req.OrgId, rbac.PermOrgUpdate) — handlers.go:58-77 checks RoleIn(A), rbac.Can and EmailVerified. req.NodeId is never bound to req.OrgId, here or in any middleware (router.go installs no node-scoping middleware).
2. nodes/service.go:2094 calls GetNodeSiteBinding{ID: N, OrgID: A} (sites.sql:60-64, whose own comment says "No rows when the node is not in this org") → pgx.ErrNoRows. bErr is consumed ONLY for `wasGateway := bErr == nil && binding.Valid` and is never returned. Execution continues into the transaction.
3. service.go:2097 → RevokeNode (nodes.sql:96-99, `WHERE org_id=$1 AND id=$2`) is declared :exec; sqlc generates `_, err := q.db.Exec(...)` (nodes.sql.go:734-737), so 0 rows matched returns nil. Org B's node stays status='active'.
4. service.go:2102 → RevokeDevicesForNode (devices.sql:137-139, `WHERE node_id=$1 AND status IN ('active','pending')`, no org predicate) revokes every active and pending device in org B homed on N, stamping revoked_cause='cascade'. The row count is discarded (`_, e :=`).
5. service.go:2107 → RevokeOVPNClientCertsForNode (ovpn.sql:66-68, also node_id-only) revokes org B's OVPN client certs. Its RETURNING org_id — which exists precisely so the right CRL can be rebuilt — is discarded, and the post-commit s.rebuildCRL(ctx, orgID) at service.go:2126 rebuilds org A's CRL, leaving org B's revoked serials off org B's CRL until the 12h scheduled rebuild.
6. audit(..., orgID=A, "node.revoked", ...) writes into org A. Org B's audit log records nothing. wasGateway is false by construction, so ReconcileHubSet never runs for org B either.

Outcome: a read-only member of org B wipes org B's device fleet homed on N — every user drops off the next DesiredState reconcile (peer/roster queries filter status='active') — while org B's node reads healthy, org B's audit log is silent, and org B's CRL is stale. Nothing self-heals: N never left 'active', so the S13.1 cascade-restore trigger never fires. The sibling paths do it correctly — RevokeDevice is :one ... WHERE id=$1 AND org_id=$2 (devices.sql:130) and SetHubPriority does an org-scoped read plus an :execrows 0-row check (service.go:1184-1198) — so this is a deviation, not a design. The two lint:cross-org annotations on the sweeps assert "org-authorized upstream", which is exactly the premise that is unmet, and querylint_test.go:139 skips annotated queries, so TestQueriesScopeOrgID is disarmed here.
ranked.why_it_matters: An authenticated, ordinary API call performs a destructive cross-tenant write with the revocation record and the revocation effect landing in different tenants — unauditable after the fact, and undetectable by the victim org. It is also the primitive the entire gone-gate rests on: revocation is supposed to be a precise, org-scoped human decision. Pre-existing on main (git diff f9b2dfd0...HEAD leaves Revoke untouched), but it sits directly under the reviewed surface and is the highest-blast-radius confirmed defect in this pass.
ranked.suggested_direction: Resolve the node inside the org before any cascade — GetNodeForOrg(nodeID, orgID) at the top of nodes.Revoke, 404 on ErrNoRows, matching SetHubPriority. Independently make RevokeNode :execrows and refuse on 0 rows, and add org predicates to RevokeDevicesForNode and RevokeOVPNClientCertsForNode so isolation is structural. Then correct the two lint:cross-org annotations to state what is actually enforced, and add a red that revokes a foreign node id and asserts node_not_found with zero device writes.

ranked.title: D3's gone-gate refuses D10's fingerprint recovery for a full 48h CertTTL — the lost re-key commit advances the exact column the gate reads
ranked.failure_sequence:
FOUR finders (binding, replay, regression, sql) found this independently; the replay, regression and sql instances survived unanimously.

State: node N, status='active', cert_serial=S1, cert_public_key=SPKI(K1), cert_not_after in the past. The agent has minted and persisted pending key K2 (main.go:812).

1. Agent submits by ident{cert_serial,S1}, CSR over K2, PoP signed with K1.
2. rekey.go:157 consumes the nonce; :168 resolves N; :175 RekeyAuthorized passes (expired); :186 Verify passes; :192 SignCSR issues S2 with NotAfter = now+CertTTL (agentca/ca.go:33,198 — 48h).
3. rekey.go:202 RekeyNode commits (nodes.sql:296-299): cert_serial=S2, cert_public_key=SPKI(K2), cert_not_after=now+48h, last_seen_at=now(). The leaf exists ONLY in the HTTP response — no column stores it, and there is no re-delivery endpoint.
4. THE RESPONSE IS LOST (dropped connection, ingress 504, agent restart). saveCreds never runs; the agent still holds the expired cert, K1, and rekey-pending-key.pem = K2.
5. Agent restarts; pendingWasOnDisk=true so it tries ident{key_fingerprint, fp(K2)} FIRST (main.go:838-844), PoP by K2.
6. resolveRekeyIdentity finds exactly one row via the 0061 generated column (nodes.sql:272-274) — the D10 lookup works exactly as designed.
7. rekey.go:175 calls RekeyAuthorized('active', now+48h, true, now). policyhealth.go:347 `certNotAfter.Before(now)` is FALSE, so :351 returns (false, "the node's certificate is still valid until … — a live gateway must never be re-keyed"). REFUSED, before Verify runs. There is no idempotent-reissue branch anywhere in Rekey, and RekeyAuthorized takes no argument that could distinguish "issued but never delivered" from "live".
8. ident{cert_serial,S1} is refused too — GetNodeByCertSerial(S1) has no row since step 3 rotated the serial.

Outcome: both identifiers are refused on every retry until now+48h. The gateway holds no usable certificate, cannot use /agent/renew (that needs the cert that expired), and main.go:70-77 runs the Recover branch BEFORE any data-plane start, so a restarted gateway never configures WireGuard for the window. It does self-heal after CertTTL (+ up to one 1h backoff), so this is a bounded 48h outage, not the permanent brick D10 removed — but the only faster remedy is the join token D10 exists to avoid (new node, site binding gone, every device re-issued). Compounding: step 3 stamped last_seen_at=now(), and the CP-side refusal log says "a live gateway" for a gateway that has never held that certificate, while the agent's own most_likely_cause (main.go:916) names revocation or pre-0057 enrolment — both wrong.

The red hides it by editing the state it observes: TestLostResponseDoesNotBrickTheGateway (rekey_integration_test.go:195-198) executes `UPDATE nodes SET cert_not_after = now() - interval '2 days'` immediately before the fingerprint attempt, justified as "what it will be by the time the agent gets here in the field" — contradicted by attemptRekey's 30s floor / 1h ceiling (main.go:779-781). That UPDATE is the defect, hand-applied. Walk Leg 7 (docs/S13-boxwalk.md:314-338) claims the retry "recovers the same node id" and is marked wire-unproven.
ranked.why_it_matters: D10, migration 0061, the generated cert_key_fingerprint column, its index and the identifier/identifier_kind columns are all justified by one property: a lost response must not cost a gateway its identity. The identity is preserved; its usability is not, for up to a full certificate lifetime, because D3's gate keys on cert_not_after and the successful-but-undelivered re-key is precisely what makes cert_not_after fresh. The two decisions were designed against each other on the one path where both are load-bearing, and the guard test's green depends on a manual mutation — the 'could this check have failed?' class this codebase already minted a law for.
ranked.suggested_direction: Decide-item, not a patch: the gate needs a third authorizing fact distinct from expiry and revocation — e.g. authorize when the presented identifier is the fingerprint of the CP's CURRENT recorded key AND the CP has no record of that certificate ever being used (a cert_confirmed_at / delivery-unconfirmed marker cleared on the node's first authenticated mTLS request), or make the response idempotent by re-serving the already-issued credential over the same key rather than issuing a new identity. Note the obvious carve-out ('authorize when the proven key is the recorded key') weakens the live-gateway refusal against a stolen-key holder, which is why it must be ruled. Whatever is chosen, delete rekey_integration_test.go:195-198 so the red is the real sequence — a second Rekey immediately after the first with no manual UPDATE.

ranked.title: The re-key throttle degenerates to ONE global 600/min bucket in every shipped topology, so any unauthenticated caller can deny gateway recovery fleet-wide
ranked.failure_sequence:
State: the shipped deployment. deploy/tunnex.yml publishes only 8443 for the api service (the mTLS agent channel); the HTTP surface is reachable ONLY through the edge nginx, which proxies `location /api/` to `http://tunnex_api` (deploy/nginx/nginx.conf:31-33). Helm is the same shape (ingress.yaml → edge Service → deployment-edge.yaml → service-api), and CP replicas default to 1 (values.yaml:78), so there is no per-pod sharding.

1. router.go:108 registers rekeyOnly(newRekeyThrottle(600)) BEFORE middleware.RealIP (router.go:110), deliberately, so clientIP() (rekeythrottle.go:87-92) reads the RAW peer address and never X-Forwarded-For.
2. In this topology the raw peer address of EVERY /api/v1/agent/rekey* request is the edge container/pod IP. There is exactly one key in t.seen for all callers on earth. No upstream brake exists: nginx.conf has no limit_req, and values.yaml:129-134 ships ingress.annotations: {}.
3. rekeyOnly (rekeythrottle.go:146-151) dispatches on r.URL.Path ONLY — not method, not body — and runs ahead of the OpenAPI validator, so the attacker needs no JSON body and no plausible identifier: 600 bare GETs to /api/v1/agent/rekey per window exhaust the bucket. Prerequisites: none. No serial, no fingerprint, no key, no account.
4. The window is fixed and lazily created (rekeythrottle.go:65-69), and the attacker's own burst creates the bucket whose `reset` defines the next boundary, so saturating at each reset is trivial and self-synchronising. (A smooth 12 req/s does NOT deny — it fills the bucket at ~t+50s leaving ~10s open; the working attack is a burst of 600 at each window start.)
5. A genuine expired gateway POSTs /agent/rekey/challenge, gets 429 + Retry-After: 60. control/rekey.go:190-192,215-217 maps that to ErrRekeyThrottled; main.go:889-903 sleeps the 30s floor, deliberately does NOT advance backoff, and `continue`s forever. Every retry lands in the same exhausted global bucket.

Outcome: gateway re-key — the entire point of EPIC 13 — is unavailable to the whole deployment for as long as the attacker keeps paying ~600 requests/minute, at no credential cost. The operator's only remaining route is minting join tokens per gateway, i.e. exactly D10's cost. Rider (same root, filed separately as LOW): because the bucket is shared, the 429 boundary is also a weak aggregate-volume signal — an attacker pacing probes across windows and binary-searching the largest rate that avoids a 429 converges on 600 minus the fleet's aggregate re-key rate, contradicting rekeythrottle.go:94-95's claim that the 429 "cannot be used to learn anything the endpoint would not otherwise tell". That leak is only obtainable while consuming the fleet's budget, i.e. while performing the DoS.
ranked.why_it_matters: rekeythrottle.go:110-111 and :123-126 already state the shared-bucket plumbing — so the topology was not unknown. What is understated by a category is the ATTACKER MODEL: the comment's consumer is "one misbehaving client THERE", a fleet peer, whereas in the reference topology there is no 'there' — every client on the internet is behind that proxy, so the honest statement is that any unauthenticated caller can consume the whole fleet's recovery allowance. The disposition was made against the wrong facts. Impact is availability only (no cert issuance, no oracle, no leak; gone-gate and PoP untouched), but it deterministically disables the recovery path this epic exists to provide. TestThrottleRefusesBeyondTheWindowBudget (rekeythrottle_test.go:25-27) asserts with a second RemoteAddr that "a different client IP must have its own budget — otherwise one attacker denies every recovering gateway" — the exact property production does not have, because in production there is no second client IP.
ranked.suggested_direction: Either (a) trusted-proxy configuration — a configured hop count / trusted CIDR set, keying the throttle off the XFF entry the trusted chain vouches for; or (b) split the budget — a small per-identifier bucket in front of the global one so a junk-identifier flood cannot starve a specific gateway; or (c) reserve headroom — cap only the RSA-reaching submit path globally and let the cheap challenge INSERT through. Whatever is ruled, amend rekeythrottle.go:94-95 and :123-126 to name the internet-caller model, and re-red the per-caller test so it exercises the shipped proxy shape rather than two synthetic RemoteAddrs.

ranked.title: attemptRekey's retry loop has no exit on persistent refusal, so the join token the operator supplied is never used and the documented remedy is unreachable
ranked.failure_sequence:
State: gateway G's key was stolen; the operator revokes node G (D3's answer to a stolen credential) and mints a join token. G's certificate later expires.

1. Operator sets TUNNEX_JOIN_TOKEN and restarts the agent.
2. identity.Decide sees an expired stored certificate and returns Action=Recover with HaveToken=true (decide.go:105-119) — Recover is returned unconditionally on expiry; haveToken only changes the Evidence string, never the Action (decide_test.go:57-63 pins this).
3. main.go:77 calls attemptRekey, whose signature (main.go:791) takes no HaveToken argument at all — the loop cannot know a fallback exists.
4. Every attempt is refused: policyhealth.go:335-338 refuses status=='revoked' unconditionally as its first check, with no expiry override, and nodes.sql:298 additionally pins RekeyNode to status='active'. There is no un-revoke statement for nodes anywhere.
5. `for attempt := 1; ; attempt++` (main.go:852) has no attempt cap and no deadline. Exhaustive enumeration of its exits: success (869), saveCreds failure after success (862-864), and `if !sleepCtx(...) { return nil,nil,nil }` at 899/924 — i.e. only when ctx is already cancelled. A persistent refusal falls to 924, sleeps, doubles the backoff toward the 1h ceiling (927-931), and re-enters the loop indefinitely.
6. main.go:82-95 — the branch literally commented "Re-key exhausted (refused persistently, or the context ended)" and its agent_falling_back_to_join_token enrolment (91-97) — is therefore never reached from a refusal. The 'context ended' half is not a route either: on SIGTERM sleepCtx returns false, control reaches enrollWithToken with an already-cancelled ctx, which fails and exits.
7. The refusal log at main.go:911-923 prints remedy = "mint a join token in the control plane and restart this agent with TUNNEX_JOIN_TOKEN set" — to a process that already has one set and will never read it. Restarting into it re-enters Recover and blocks in the same loop.

Same loop strands a second, larger population: nodes enrolled before migration 0057 have no recorded key, so RekeyAuthorized's !certNotAfterKnown branch (policyhealth.go:341) refuses forever with no operator action available — and they hit the identical infinite loop with a valid token sitting in the environment.
ranked.why_it_matters: This re-creates EPIC 11 WF-S11-11 — the bug identity/decide.go was written to fix (operator supplies a token, agent ignores it and loops forever) — one layer further in, and it breaks D3's story end to end: policyhealth.go:322-324 and docs/S13.1-decisions.md D1 both state that a revoked gateway recovers through an operator-minted join token, and the agent structurally cannot take that path. The fallback branch is live for the cases where re-key is locally IMPOSSIBLE (unreadable serial, pending-key persist/parse failure, saveCreds failure) and dead for exactly the case its own comment names. No test covers attemptRekey's loop exit.
ranked.suggested_direction: Pass the token's presence into attemptRekey and bound the refusal path when and only when a token exists — return after N consecutive non-throttle refusals, or once the backoff first reaches the ceiling — so control falls through to enrollWithToken while ctx is still live. Keep the unbounded loop for the token-less case, which is what the ceiling comment at main.go:766-780 is actually reasoning about. ErrRekeyThrottled must not count toward that bound (review #10).

ranked.title: The agent fixes its identity list before the retry loop, so the process that suffered the lost response never tries the fingerprint identity at all
ranked.failure_sequence:
Two finders (replay, regression) found this independently; all four verdicts confirmed it.

1. Agent boots with an expired certificate and no rekey-pending-key.pem. attemptRekey calls loadOrCreatePendingKey (main.go:812), which MINTS K2, writes it temp-then-rename, and returns wasOnDisk=FALSE (main.go:489-493).
2. `identities` is built ONCE at main.go:837-849, outside the loop that starts at main.go:852. Because pendingWasOnDisk is false, the fingerprint entry is skipped and identities contains ONLY {CertSerial: S1}.
3. Attempt 1 submits by serial. The CP commits (RekeyNode rotates cert_serial to S2 and records SPKI(K2), nodes.sql:296-299) and the response is lost. The agent process does NOT restart.
4. control.Rekey returns a transport error; the loop backs off and continues.
5. Every subsequent attempt, forever, iterates the same one-element slice and re-submits S1, which GetNodeByCertSerial (nodes.sql:32-33) resolves to zero rows → uniform refusal. K2 is on disk and is exactly what the CP now records, and the agent never asks about it. Even the PoP would fail: the serial attempt signs with keyPEM (K1) while the CP's recorded key is now K2.
6. Backoff caps at rekeyBackoffCeiling = 1h. attemptRekey never returns, so nothing exits; serveHealth (main.go:49,384-388) always answers 200 on liveness while readiness stays false, so Kubernetes will not restart the pod. The refusal log even prints identities_tried = 1 (main.go:912).

Waiting does not help this process: unlike the restarted case, the 48h cert expiry is irrelevant because S1 matches no row at any time. Recovery requires an out-of-band restart that nothing triggers — and after a restart the agent then hits the 48h gate collision reported separately. Note the mitigating fact both lenses established: recomputing the flag per iteration would NOT make attempt 2 succeed, because the fresh 48h cert_not_after makes the gate refuse the fingerprint too; the difference is delayed automatic recovery versus a silent permanent in-process brick.
ranked.why_it_matters: The pending key is persisted before submit specifically so a lost response is survivable, but the flag that decides whether to USE it is sampled before the first submit and never refreshed. The exact case D10 was built for is the case where the mechanism stays switched off for the lifetime of the process, and the comment at main.go:825-831 asserts the opposite ("it tries both, and each attempt is independently sound"). Walk Leg 7 is wire-unproven, and main_test.go covers only the disk semantics of loadOrCreatePendingKey — nothing drives attemptRekey across attempts.
ranked.suggested_direction: Decide the identity list per attempt rather than once, or set a `submitted` bool after the first control.Rekey call and unconditionally include the fingerprint identity thereafter — once a request has gone out, the CP may hold that key, which is the fingerprint identity's only precondition. The 'skip on first attempt' optimisation should be scoped to 'before any request has been sent', not 'the key was not on disk at function entry'. Red: let attempt 1 fail after the CP commits, assert attempt 2 tries the fingerprint.

ranked.title: Post-commit device restore has no node-status guard, so a re-key that races an operator revoke re-activates the devices that revoke just cascaded
ranked.failure_sequence:
Two finders (replay, gate) found this independently; both survived with one lens each arguing the severity down (not the mechanism).

Rekey does its work in two transactions with an unsynchronised gap and never re-reads node.Status after the commit.

1. A re-key passes the gate (rekey.go:175), verifies, signs, and its transaction COMMITS at rekey.go:237. N is active with a fresh certificate.
2. Before rekey.go:254 runs, the operator revokes N: nodes/service.go:2096-2111 commits RevokeNode (status='revoked') + RevokeDevicesForNode (devices.sql:137-139 → all 40 devices status='revoked', revoked_cause='cascade') + RevokeOVPNClientCertsForNode, then rebuildCRL. The operator gets 204 and believes the gateway and its users are dead. Revoke takes NO advisory lock, so it does not serialise against step 3 — and because a revoke issued while the re-key tx is still open BLOCKS on the nodes row lock held by RekeyNode (nodes.sql:298), concurrency funnels it into precisely this window.
3. rekey.go:254 calls restoreDevices(ctx, node.OrgID, node.ID) → devices/restore.go:50. It takes LockDeviceKey and runs ListCascadeRevokedDevicesForNode (devices.sql:293-296, keyed on node_id + cause='cascade', with NO join or predicate on the node's status). devices.Service.withTx uses READ COMMITTED, so the SELECT sees the revoke that committed while it was blocked on the lock. RestoreCascadeRevokedDevice (devices.sql:314-316) sets each row back to status='active', clears revoked_at and revoked_cause (destroying the cascade evidence), reallocates addresses, and writes device.restored audit rows with cause='gateway_recovered'. restore.go then pushes fleet-wide.

Outcome: node N is revoked, its 40 device credentials are active again holding pool addresses and counting against caps, appearing in ListActiveDeviceAllocations and re-homable under S8.6, with an audit trail asserting a gateway recovery the operator explicitly countermanded and no audit row explaining the reversal. Scoping both lenses established: policy transit through the revoked gateway is NOT restored (Slice 2 filters revoked nodes from the compiler input) and the OVPN certs stay revoked/CRL'd, so it is a device-tier and audit-integrity reversal rather than restored tunnel access; and a repeat revoke re-cascades them, since RevokeDevicesForNode ignores revoked_cause.

Critical rider (see the separate critic-unverified finding): revoked_cause='cascade' is written by exactly ONE statement whose only caller sets the node revoked in the same transaction, and a revoked node can never pass RekeyAuthorized or RekeyNode's status='active' CAS — so in the ABSENCE of this race the re-key-path restore can never find a candidate. This interleaving is the only state in which the re-key call site's restore does anything at all, which changes the disposition from 'narrow the window' to 'this call site has no benign execution'.
ranked.why_it_matters: D3's premise is that revocation is a human decision no mechanical proof may overturn. The gate protects the NODE row correctly (RekeyAuthorized + RekeyNode's status='active' CAS); the device tier has no equivalent — restore is authorised by a decision taken before the commit and applied after it, against state that may have changed. A revoke that returns 204 while a background goroutine puts the devices back is the worst shape of the class: the operator has positive confirmation the action succeeded. restore_integration_test.go seeds every fixture device active under an active node, a combination production can only reach through this race.
ranked.suggested_direction: Make the restore conditional on the node still being active at restore time, inside the restore transaction: re-read the node under LockDeviceKey and abort when status != 'active', or add `AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM nodes n WHERE n.id = devices.node_id AND n.status = 'active')` to BOTH ListCascadeRevokedDevicesForNode and RestoreCascadeRevokedDevice so the guard is construction, matching RekeyNode's own status clause. Given the reachability rider, first rule on whether the re-key call site should exist at all — removing it deletes the race outright.

ranked.title: Cascade restore promotes NEVER-APPROVED (pending) devices to 'active', silently bypassing the device-approval gate — the pre-cascade status is never recorded
ranked.failure_sequence:
Two finders (gate, sql) found this independently; both survived, with one lens each arguing reachability/severity down.

State: enterprise org with organizations.device_approval='on'. Alice enrols laptop D on gateway G; devices/service.go:261-263 sets deviceStatus='pending' (`s.approvalEnforced && org.DeviceApproval == "on"`), and CreateDevice binds node_id AND assigned_ip at creation, not at approval. D sits in ListPendingDevicesByOrg awaiting an admin.

1. Operator revokes G. RevokeDevicesForNode (devices.sql:137-139) sweeps `status IN ('active','pending')` → D becomes status='revoked', revoked_cause='cascade', assigned_ip PRESERVED (the 0059 change). THE PRIOR STATUS IS RECORDED NOWHERE: migration 0059 adds only revoked_cause, and the node.revoked audit meta is empty (nodes/service.go:2109). After the sweep a never-approved pending row and an approved active row are byte-identical in every column the restore reads.
2. A restore runs against G. ListCascadeRevokedDevicesForNode (devices.sql:293-296) selects only on status='revoked' AND revoked_cause='cascade' — it neither records nor filters on the prior status, and restore.go never reads org.DeviceApproval (it reads the org solely for PoolCidr).
3. RestoreCascadeRevokedDevice (devices.sql:314-316) executes `SET status='active', revoked_at=NULL, revoked_cause=NULL, assigned_ip=$2, node_id=$3` unconditionally. approved_by stays NULL.

Outcome: an enrolment no admin ever approved is status='active' with approved_by IS NULL — indistinguishable from 0020's grandfathered rows. It enters ListActiveWireGuardPeersForNode and the policy compiler's ListActiveDevicesForOrg (both gate on status='active'; nothing anywhere reads approved_by for enforcement), gets a peer slot and a /32, and DISAPPEARS from ListPendingDevicesByOrg so the admin never sees it again and cannot RejectDevice (devices.sql:18-25 requires status='pending'). restore_integration_test.go's addDevice hard-codes status='active' for every fixture, and the sweep helper's own comment at line 78-86 names 'pending' — the case is named and untested.
ranked.why_it_matters: Device approval is the org's stated control over which endpoints get a credential (0020: 'an org-level device-approval gate'). The restore statement asserts a terminal value ('active') for a set whose members were not all active, and nothing in the schema retained what they were — the same 'two facts render identically' problem revoked_cause was added to fix, one column over. The epic's thesis is that a mechanical event must never overturn a human decision; 'pending' is the absence of one.
ranked.suggested_direction: Record the pre-cascade status so restore can return each row to it — add revoked_from_status alongside revoked_cause in the 0059 family (RevokeDevicesForNode writes `revoked_from_status = status`) and have RestoreCascadeRevokedDevice restore to it. Minimum acceptable: `SET status = CASE WHEN approved_by IS NULL AND <org requires approval> THEN 'pending' ELSE 'active' END`. Red: seed a pending device, cascade it, restore, assert it is back in the approval queue. Do NOT simply exclude pending rows from the candidate set — that strands them revoked-with-cause forever, invisible to both the queue and RejectDevice.

ranked.title: Restored OpenVPN devices come back 'active' with their client certificates still revoked and on the org CRL — restore reverses one of the three acts revoke performs
ranked.failure_sequence:
Two finders (gate, sql) found this independently; all four verdicts confirmed it.

State: org O with OpenVPN devices homed on gateway G; device D has transport='openvpn' and an ovpn_client_certs row (serial X, not_after = issued + ovpnca.ClientCertTTL = 365 days, ca.go:39). The client private key was returned once and is NOT stored server-side.

1. G is revoked. nodes/service.go:2100-2110 runs, in one transaction, RevokeDevicesForNode (D → revoked, cause='cascade') AND RevokeOVPNClientCertsForNode (ovpn.sql:66-68 → revoked_at=now() for serial X); service.go:2126 then rebuilds the org CRL, publishing X (ListRevokedOVPNSerialsByOrg, ovpn.sql:19-21, keeps it while not_after > now()). crl-verify is unconditional on the gateway (ovpnserver.go:274-277, re-checked at reneg :252).
2. A restore runs against G — reachable today via POST /organizations/{orgId}/nodes/{nodeId}/restore-devices (node_handlers.go:138-146) with a live replacement target.
3. ListCascadeRevokedDevicesForNode (devices.sql:293-296) returns D and SELECTs `transport` — restore.go never references it (grep: zero hits in the file). RestoreCascadeRevokedDevice sets D back to status='active'. Nothing in restore.go touches ovpn_client_certs; there is NO un-revoke statement for them anywhere in the repo (`revoked_at = NULL` appears only in devices.sql:315); restore.go never calls RebuildCRL, and the 12h scheduled rebuild re-affirms the block rather than clearing it.

Outcome: D reappears in ListActiveOVPNDevicesForNode (devices.sql:255-262, gated on status='active'), so the gateway is handed a CCD entry and a /32 and the API renders it healthy — needs_reexport is even false when the address was kept, because provisioned_ip == assigned_ip. But the gateway's crl-verify rejects serial X on every connection for the remaining cert lifetime (up to a year). There is no remedy: ovpn.Service.ExportProfile has one caller (ovpn_handlers.go:94) which CREATES A NEW DEVICE first — no per-device re-issue exists, and the key was never persisted — so the only fix is delete-and-recreate, precisely the fleet-wide re-issue event Wall 6 / D5 exist to avoid. On the operator path the restored device is also re-homed to a different gateway, so its .ovpn profile still embeds the dead gateway's `remote` — unusable on two independent grounds. The restore reports restored=N and logs success.

The standing who-reads-this probe fires exactly here: `transport` is a field added to a query with no consuming line.
ranked.why_it_matters: Revocation of an OpenVPN device is a three-part act (devices + ovpn_client_certs + CRL) that the node-revoke path performs correctly as 'the SHARED seam'. The restore reverses one third, producing a state no revoke/restore pair should reach: control plane green, data plane refusing, operator told it succeeded. This is the reassuring-green class the codebase has repeatedly ruled against, reproduced inside the fix for Wall 6 — a fleet-wide user event invisible until people call.
ranked.suggested_direction: Restore must be the inverse of the sweep it undoes: add an un-revoke for ovpn_client_certs guarded to clear revoked_at only for certs revoked by the cascade (never by a deliberate device revoke) inside the restore transaction, and call RebuildCRL(orgID) after commit via the same shared seam both revoke paths use. If reinstating a revoked serial is judged incoherent — and for the re-home case a fresh cert against the new gateway's remotes is needed anyway — then restore must refuse or flag transport='openvpn' candidates as needing re-issue and exclude them from restored=N, rather than returning them to the roster. Either way `transport` must be read or removed from the SELECT. Do not land the un-revoke before the post-commit race above is closed, or a re-key could clear serials off a CRL an operator just published.

ranked.title: The agent maps every non-200/429 status — and every transport error — to a PERMANENT refusal, so a control-plane blip prints the destructive 'mint a join token' remedy
ranked.failure_sequence:
State: a gateway's certificate has expired and it is in attemptRekey's loop. The control plane is rolled/restarted, its ingress answers 502/503/504, or the API returns 500 (a DB failover, the NUL path below, or any unmapped error through apierr.Write — rekey.go:58,70,94,102,164,220,238 all return unmapped errors, and apierr.go:62-70 renders them 500).

1. rekeyChallenge (control/rekey.go:215-220) or Rekey (control/rekey.go:190-195) sees resp.StatusCode != 200 and — having special-cased ONLY 429 on the line above — returns ErrRekeyRefused. The same applies to a raw transport error from client.Do (control/rekey.go:186-188, 211-213): connection refused, TLS failure, or the 20s timeout, i.e. the commonest shape of a restarting control plane, is neither ErrRekeyThrottled nor a status and falls through identically.
2. attemptRekey's throttle branch (main.go:891) does not match, so control falls to main.go:906-925, which logs agent_rekey_refused with server_said = "refused, without a reason", most_likely_cause = "enrolled before the control plane recorded agent public keys … or it was REVOKED, which re-key deliberately cannot undo", and remedy = "mint a join token in the control plane and restart this agent with TUNNEX_JOIN_TOKEN set" — when the server said nothing at all.
3. main.go:927-931 doubles the backoff toward the 1h ceiling. (Correction from verification: a 30s blip costs one failed attempt plus one 30s sleep, not an hour; reaching the ceiling needs ~7-8 consecutive failures, i.e. hours of real outage.)
4. An operator following the printed remedy enrols with a join token — which main.go:93 itself describes as creating a NEW node: site binding gone, devices needing re-issue. Note the agent does not do this automatically: the loop never returns on refusal (see the join-token finding above), so the harm is the misleading operator-facing diagnosis that invites the identity-destroying remedy.

Trigger correlation: a fleet whose certificates all expired during an outage recovers precisely while the control plane is being restarted, so the misdiagnosis fires at the worst moment. Review #10 already ruled this exact shape a defect and fixed it for 429 only; docs/S13.1-decisions.md:882-883 asserts the agent 'already distinguishes the two', which is true only for 429.
ranked.why_it_matters: The endpoint's uniform-refusal discipline is about the BODY; the status code is the one signal the agent may legitimately branch on, and it does not. A permanent-refusal diagnosis printed during a transient outage is how an operator is talked into discarding a gateway identity that was fine. The 403 the CP actually uses for refusal is distinguishable from a 5xx, a 404 and a dead socket, and the agent currently treats all four the same.
ranked.suggested_direction: Reserve the refusal diagnosis for the status the CP uses for it (403 rekey_refused). Add a transient/unavailable class covering 5xx, unexpected statuses AND transport errors, classified at the main.go:891/908 fork rather than only at control/rekey.go:193 — retried, not escalated toward the ceiling, logged with the status, and never printing the join-token remedy. 404 should stay in the permanent class (a path-prefix misconfiguration is not transient), but must log its status.

ranked.title: saveCreds leaves a NEW certificate beside an OLD key on interruption — the exact state its comment claims to prevent — and the agent then os.Exit(1)s forever
ranked.failure_sequence:
1. Re-key (main.go:861), renewal (main.go:510) or token enrolment (main.go:974) succeeds; saveCreds(dir, newCert /*over K2*/, K2, ca) runs.
2. The loop at main.go:441 renames in the deterministic order ca.pem, cert.pem, key.pem, each as WriteFile(tmp) then Rename. Between the cert.pem rename and the key.pem rename sits a full os.WriteFile of key.pem.tmp — a real window of create+write+close syscalls during which the directory holds cert.pem = NEW certificate (binding K2) and key.pem = OLD key K1. There is no fsync of the files or the directory, so under power loss the ordering is not even guaranteed.
3. The process is killed there (SIGKILL, OOM, eviction, power loss).
4. On restart loadCreds succeeds (it reads the three files independently and never compares them). identity.Decide is called with certPEM only (main.go:55) — it never receives keyPEM — parses a NotAfter 48h in the future, and returns UseStored (decide.go:143).
5. control.NewClient calls tls.X509KeyPair(certPEM, keyPEM) (client.go:90), which fails with "private key does not match public key". This is the only pair validation anywhere in apps/node.
6. main.go:152-156 logs agent_client_failed and calls os.Exit(1) → CrashLoopBackOff, contradicting the rule the same file states twice at main.go:95-99 and :129 ("an agent must never exit on a condition that a control-plane change could resolve") and which every sibling branch honours by idling.
7. Every restart repeats 4-6. The Recover branch is gated on expiry (decide.go:106) so re-key is not attempted for the remaining certificate lifetime.

Blast radius depends on the call site: on the re-key path K2 also survives in rekey-pending-key.pem (removed only after the last rename, main.go:450+), so the gateway self-heals once the cert expires. On the renewLoop and enrollWithToken paths K2 exists ONLY in memory and the un-renamed key.pem.tmp — the kill destroys it permanently, and when the cert finally expires the agent can only prove possession of K1 while the CP recorded K2, so BOTH re-key identities are refused forever and only a join token (new node, lost site binding) recovers it.

The doc comment at main.go:428-430 states the property this ordering is supposed to give — "if the sequence is interrupted, the old key still matches the old certificate" — which is false for this order, since cert.pem has already moved. Review #3 replaced a randomised map-range with this deterministic order and claimed crash-atomicity; it made the hazard deterministic rather than removing it, and picked the branch where the agent cannot diagnose itself and hard-exits. TestSaveCredsClearsThePendingKey (main_test.go:120) passes literal []byte("cert")/[]byte("key") and never parses the pair.
ranked.why_it_matters: No two-file rename sequence is atomic, so no ordering delivers the claimed property — key-first would leave key.pem=K2 beside a cert binding K1, equally fatal. The real defects are downstream: the agent has no boot-time pair check, and it treats an unusable local credential set as fatal rather than as exactly the kind of condition a control-plane action could resolve. A microsecond interruption costs a gateway a certificate lifetime, or its identity outright.
ranked.suggested_direction: Make the credential set one atomic unit (write ca/cert/key into a sibling temp directory and rename the directory, or one combined file loadCreds parses), and fsync files + directory. Independently, and required either way: (a) verify the pair with tls.X509KeyPair immediately after loadCreds and give identity.Decide a fourth verdict for a mismatched pair, preferring the pending key when it pairs with cert.pem so the re-key case heals on the next boot rather than after 48h; (b) delete the os.Exit(1) at main.go:155 and idle per the rule the same commit established; (c) correct the comment at main.go:428-430.

ranked.title: A NUL byte in cert_serial provokes a raw PostgreSQL encoding error on BOTH unauthenticated re-key routes — 500 instead of the uniform 403
ranked.failure_sequence:
Two finders (oracle, errors) found this independently; all four verdicts confirmed it, two of them by execution against the running stack.

POST /api/v1/agent/rekey/challenge with body {"cert_serial":"�"} (the JSON ESCAPE — a raw 0x00 byte is rejected by encoding/json before it reaches the parser).
1. rekeyOnly (rekeythrottle.go:146) caps the body and admits it.
2. The OpenAPI validator passes: cert_serial is `type: string, maxLength: 100` with no pattern (openapi.yaml:3103-3105, 3131) and kin-openapi does no charset check. Verified by running the real GetSwagger spec through openapi3filter.ValidateRequest: nil for both routes; the decoder yields a real 0x00 byte.
3. ParseRekeyIdentifier (rekeyident.go:58-61) takes the `certSerial != ""` branch and returns {Kind:"cert_serial", Value:"\x00"}, true — the value is never inspected; only the fingerprint branch validates charset (rekeyident.go:63-66).
4. IssueRekeyChallenge passes the kind switch (rekey.go:48-52) and the non-empty check (:53), then INSERTs the identifier as a text parameter (nodes.sql:219-220). PostgreSQL refuses NUL in a UTF-8 text value — verified against tunnex-postgres-1: `ERROR: invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8": 0x00 (SQLSTATE 22021)` on both `SELECT $1::text` and the real INSERT.
5. rekey.go:70 returns that error RAW; node_handlers.go:163-165 passes it through; apierr.Write (apierr.go:60-70) finds no *apierr.Error and renders 500 {"code":"internal_error"} plus one ERROR-level log line carrying the full PG error.

The submit route is identical and needs nothing else valid: {"cert_serial":"�","nonce":"","csr":"","signature":"","agent_version":"x"} → ConsumeRekeyChallenge (rekey.go:157) errors with SQLSTATE 22021, which is not pgx.ErrNoRows, so rekey.go:164 returns it raw → 500. No nonce, no CSR, no key, no real serial required — the parameter fails at Bind, before resolve, before the gate, before any crypto.

Scoping both lenses established: this is NOT an oracle. The 500 is a pure function of the caller's own bytes and fires identically for a live, revoked, expired, unknown or ambiguous identifier, so nothing about the fleet leaks. What it breaks is the stated contract (openapi.yaml:1880-1882, 'Every failure returns the SAME refusal'; D8's uniform 403) plus unauthenticated ERROR-log amplification bounded at 600/min per source address — on the challenge route, which otherwise logs nothing per request, that is a cheap outsider-driven 500-rate alarm generator. No pool poisoning (the failing statements run outside withTx).
ranked.why_it_matters: This is the exact sibling of the defect already fixed in this file — an unrecognised identifier_kind reaching the CHECK constraint and returning 500 (rekey.go:42-52). The parser validates the KIND but not the VALUE, and the cert_serial branch inspects nothing at all, so a value the schema explicitly permits reaches a text bind parameter the database cannot store. TestBothIdentifiersRefuseIndistinguishably (rekey_integration_test.go:220) enumerates six well-formed cases and would go red the moment a NUL-bearing serial is added.
ranked.suggested_direction: Validate the identifier VALUE at the parse layer: reject any cert_serial containing 0x00 (or any non-graphic control byte, or simply require hex — serials are produced by agentca.serialString) in ParseRekeyIdentifier's certSerial branch, returning the same `false` a malformed fingerprint returns so it lands on ErrRekeyRefused for BOTH routes at one point. Add the NUL case to TestBothIdentifiersRefuseIndistinguishably. Do NOT blanket-map DB errors to 403 — that hides a real control-plane outage behind a refusal the agent reads as permanent.

ranked.title: Moving the throttle above the access-log middleware made every 429 invisible server-side — no log line, no X-Request-Id, no source address
ranked.failure_sequence:
1. Before the fix the throttle was registered at the bottom of the chain (commit 8cccfb0, after applog.Requests), so a 429 produced a normal http_request access-log line and carried X-Request-ID. Verified via `git show 8cccfb0 -- apps/api/internal/http/router.go`.
2. The fix re-registered it at router.go:108, above middleware.RealIP (110), corsBearer (116), applog.Requests (118), middleware.Recoverer (119) and the Cache-Control:no-store middleware (124).
3. A caller — or a NAT/ingress aggregating a whole fleet into one bucket, which per the finding above is EVERY shipped topology — exceeds 600 requests/min on the re-key routes.
4. rekeyThrottle.throttled (rekeythrottle.go:98-104) writes 429 via http.Error and returns WITHOUT calling next. applog.Requests (log/log.go:44-62) — the only code in the repo that sets X-Request-ID and emits the http_request line — never runs. rekeythrottle.go imports only net, net/http, sync, time: no logger is reachable from the refusal path, and no test asserts anything about it.
5. Recovering gateways log agent_rekey_throttled on their side (main.go:891-897); the control plane logs nothing. An operator asked "why is the fleet not recovering?" sees a silent CP with no evidence any request was refused, no source addresses, and no request ids to correlate against the agents' reports.

Corrections from verification, which narrow but do not remove it: there is no per-request HTTP metric for ANY route at any chain position (metrics.go exposes only gateway policy health and scheduler leader), so 'no metric' is not a regression; corsBearer also short-circuits above applog, so this is not the only pre-log short-circuit; and a fronting proxy — the precondition for the fleet-starvation scenario — does log the 429 externally. The precise loss is the CP-side access-log line and the request id.
ranked.why_it_matters: The one endpoint pair on the API that is unauthenticated by construction is now the only one whose refusals leave no server-side trace, and it is refused from a bucket that the shipped topology makes global. Fleet-wide recovery starvation is therefore undiagnosable from the control plane's own logs — the operator cannot even confirm that refusals are happening, let alone from where.
ranked.suggested_direction: Keep the registration order — the RealIP and pre-validator body-cap positioning is load-bearing — and give the throttle its own visibility: emit a structured log line from inside throttled (it has r.RemoteAddr and r.URL.Path in hand: path, raw peer IP, bucket count) and/or a counter in internal/metrics. Setting X-Request-ID from middleware.GetReqID before writing the 429 is a cheap complement.

ranked.title: Cascade restore reclaims an address no longer inside the org pool, because 0059 stopped clearing assigned_ip and the pool-shrink orphan check cannot see revoked rows
ranked.failure_sequence:
State: org O with pool_cidr = 10.10.0.0/24. Device D on gateway G holds assigned_ip = 10.10.0.200.

1. G is revoked. Since S13.1, RevokeDevicesForNode (devices.sql:137-139) KEEPS assigned_ip — pre-0059 it set it NULL. D is now revoked, cause='cascade', assigned_ip = 10.10.0.200. Migration 0059's justification is explicit: 'the two readers that define this address is taken both filter on status'.
2. An admin shrinks the pool to 10.10.0.0/25. The orphan check in ResizePool (devices/service.go:512-546) reads ListActiveDeviceAllocations, which filters `status IN ('active','pending')` — D is revoked and therefore invisible. ipalloc.Orphans sees no address above .127, the resize is accepted, UpdateOrgPoolCidr commits.
3. G's devices are restored (reachable today via the operator endpoint). restore.go builds `taken` ONLY from ListActiveDeviceAllocations. old = "10.10.0.200"; taken[old] is false — nobody holds it, it is not even in the pool. The branch at restore.go:131 is `if old == "" || taken[old]`, which is false, so ipalloc.Allocate(org.PoolCidr, used) — the ONLY place the pool is consulted, and the only place p.Contains(a) would have applied (ipalloc.go:48) — is never reached. There is no containment test on the reclaim path.
4. RestoreCascadeRevokedDevice writes assigned_ip='10.10.0.200', status='active', and the result is reported KeptAddress: true, audited as device.restored (not device.restored_readdressed), with needs_reexport false because provisioned_ip == assigned_ip.

Outcome: an active device holds a /32 outside the org's pool. The gateway's wg0 is 10.10.0.1/25 and every other peer's AllowedIPs is the /25, so peer-to-peer traffic to .200 has no route; site links advertise the pool CIDR, so site→device return traffic blackholes. devices_org_ip_key is UNIQUE(org_id, assigned_ip) WHERE status IN ('active','pending') — uniqueness, not containment — so nothing objects. The shrink's stated guarantee ('no active device outside the pool') is silently violated after the fact by a gateway event. The same hole covers ipalloc's second orphan class: a reclaimed address numerically inside the new pool but landing on its reserved network/gateway/broadcast slot is restored unchecked, since Orphans only ever sees active/pending rows.
ranked.why_it_matters: 0059's argument for keeping assigned_ip is sound for taken-ness, but the reclaim path asks a DIFFERENT question — is this address still valid for this org? — and asks only the taken-ness oracle. The shrink guard and the restore reclaim now disagree about which rows exist, and the resulting device is broken in a way that reads clean on every surface: KeptAddress true, no readdressed audit, no re-export signal. TestResizePoolShrinkRefusesOrphans and TestRestoreReclaimsTheOriginalAddressWhenFree each pass; the two features were never composed in a red.
ranked.suggested_direction: Fold containment into the reclaim branch — `if old == "" || taken[old] || !poolContains(org.PoolCidr, old)` — reusing ipalloc's own containment + reserved-slot logic so 'still valid for this org' has one definition; falling through to Allocate already drives kept=false, the readdressed audit and needs_reexport. Separately rule whether ResizePool's orphan census should include cascade-revoked rows, since they are restorable and therefore not free.

ranked.title: The Wall-6 restore at the re-key call site is unreachable by construction, and its only reachable execution is the race that undoes an operator's revoke — the comment justifying it claims the opposite
ranked.failure_sequence:
UNVERIFIED — raised by the completeness critic; no adversarial lens ran on it. It is the disposition-changing rider on the post-commit-restore race above, and both lenses on that race independently reached the same reachability conclusion, so the underlying facts are corroborated.

Two halves of one change set assert opposite reachability. rekey.go:243-252 justifies the post-commit s.restoreDevices call: "WALL 6 (S13.1 D5): revoking a gateway cascades to every device homed on it, so recovery WITHOUT this step hands back a working gateway with ZERO users, each needing a re-issued one-time config" — repeated at cmd/server/main.go:255-256, with rekey.go:261 logging devices_restored_after_rekey. But devices/restore.go:56-60, in the same change set, states the reverse: "The second exists because the first could never fire. Devices are cascade-revoked only by nodes.Revoke, and re-key REFUSES a revoked node (D3) — so the only trigger that creates this work put the node into the one state that could never reach the code which undoes it."

restore.go is the correct one:
1. revoked_cause='cascade' is written by exactly ONE statement, RevokeDevicesForNode (devices.sql:137-139).
2. That query has exactly ONE non-test caller, nodes/service.go:2102, inside nodes.Revoke's transaction, which in the same tx sets the node status='revoked'.
3. RekeyAuthorized refuses status=='revoked' unconditionally (policyhealth.go:336-340), and RekeyNode's own WHERE is status='active' (nodes.sql:298).
4. There is no un-revoke for nodes; RestoreCascadedDevicesByOperator moves devices to a DIFFERENT active target and clears the cause.

So at the instant rekey.go:254 runs, the node was status='active' at the commit (rekey.go:237), and ListCascadeRevokedDevicesForNode can return rows in EXACTLY ONE state: an operator revoke that landed between the commit at :237 and the restore call at :254.

Wrong outcome (a): the promise is false in the case an operator will actually hit. Operator revokes gw-a (its 40 devices go revoked/cascade); operator rebuilds the box from the same state volume; the agent restarts, Decide says Recover, attemptRekey submits — and the CP refuses at policyhealth.go:336 because the node is revoked. Line 253 is never reached; the devices stay revoked. An operator reading rekey.go:243-252 during an outage believes gateway recovery brings the users back; it cannot, ever. Wall 6 is closed only by the separate operator endpoint, which requires naming a DIFFERENT active replacement gateway plus device:restore — a fact no log line, no refusal message and no comment on the re-key path states.

Wrong outcome (b): 100% of the reachable executions are harmful — the post-commit revoke race, which silently re-activates the devices the operator's revoke just cascaded. That is not a rare hazard in otherwise-useful code; it is the code's entire reachable behaviour.
ranked.why_it_matters: This codebase has a dormant-machinery law precisely because a mechanism that is correct but unreachable reads as shipped protection. Here the two halves of one change set assert opposite reachability, the false one is at the call site an operator reads during an outage, and the true one is buried in the callee. It also inverts the risk calculus on the race: with no benign execution to preserve, the correct fix there is removal, not window-narrowing.
ranked.suggested_direction: Verify, then rule. If confirmed: remove the restoreDevices call from Rekey and the SetRestoreDevices wiring (main.go:257-271) — the race disappears with it — and replace the WALL 6 comment at rekey.go:243-252 with the statement restore.go:56-60 already makes. Make the agent-facing and operator-facing refusal for a revoked node name the real remedy (join token for the gateway, then operator device-restore onto the replacement). If the call is kept, it must re-read the node's status inside the restore transaction.

ranked.title: Gate-before-crypto removes only one direction of the timing difference, and rekeyorder_test's comment vouches for equal-cost refusals the code does not deliver
ranked.failure_sequence:
Inputs: a caller holding a candidate identifier (a cert serial, or a key fingerprint computed from a stolen state volume), their own RSA keypair, and a valid self-signed CSR over it.

1. POST /agent/rekey/challenge {cert_serial: S}. Always 200 — rekey.go:42-73 never touches `nodes`.
2. POST /agent/rekey {cert_serial: S, nonce, csr: <their own valid CSR>, signature: <junk>, agent_version:"x"}. Always 403.
3. The server path splits, and only one branch does asymmetric work:
   - S unknown → nonce consumed (rekey.go:157), GetNodeByCertSerial no rows (:88-92), return. ZERO asymmetric crypto.
   - S names a LIVE node → gate refuses at policyhealth.go:351. ZERO asymmetric crypto.

ranked.title: The issuer accepts CSR public keys the proof-of-possession verifier can never accept, so a non-RSA key silently and permanently disables that node's automated recovery
ranked.failure_sequence:
rekey.Verify (rekey/pop.go:80-86) REQUIRES the STORED key to be *rsa.PublicKey and refuses anything else, with a comment explaining why it narrowed. Nothing anywhere inspects the CSR's public key: pop.go:88-100 parses the CSR and checks only its self-signature, and agentca.SignCSR (ca.go:186-217) checks PEM decode, parse and self-signature, then passes csr.PublicKey straight into x509.CreateCertificate. SignCSR is the only chokepoint and has three callers — Enroll (service.go:288), Renew (service.go:335), Rekey (rekey.go:192).

1. Node N is expired, cert_public_key = SPKI(RSA K1). A client that is not the shipped agent (a hand-rolled recovery script, a third-party or older build, a GitOps tool) submits ident{cert_serial,S1}, a valid PoP signed with K1, and a CSR over an ECDSA P-256 key E.
2. Verified by execution: `[ecdsa] CheckSignature: <nil>  CreateCertificate: <nil>  MarshalPKIX: <nil> len 91` — pop.go:98 passes, pop.go:103 verifies against K1, ca.go:202 signs the EC leaf, ca.go:208 marshals SPKI(E).
3. rekey.go:205 writes cert_public_key = base64(SPKI(E)). N works normally over mTLS and renews — service.go:343 re-records SPKI(E) on every renewal, so it NEVER self-heals.
4. N later expires. Every re-key attempt now dies at pop.go:80-86 with 'stored key is not RSA' → ErrProofInvalid → the uniform ErrRekeyRefused. Agent, operator and log-reader see the same refusal as a REVOKED node. The node is permanently outside PoP recovery and nothing ever said so; recovery falls back to the join token (D1(a)), i.e. the pre-S13.1 status quo — new node, site binding gone, devices re-issued.

The key-STRENGTH half of the original finding is REFUTED by execution: apps/api/go.mod declares go 1.25.12, so crypto/rsa's minimum-key-size rule is in force — a real 512-bit openssl CSR errors at ca.go:190 CheckSignature, at pop.go:98 and at pop.go:103 (`crypto/rsa: 512-bit keys are insecure`), so no downgraded factorable recovery credential can ever be issued. Reachability is also bounded: rekey.go:185 Verify runs BEFORE rekey.go:192 SignCSR, so injecting a chosen key into cert_public_key requires already holding the node's current private key. The property is pre-existing and CA-wide (git show f9b2dfd0:ca.go has the identical unconstrained CreateCertificate), affecting Enroll and Renew equally.
ranked.why_it_matters: The asymmetry is the tell: the verifier deliberately narrowed to RSA and wrote down why ('it keeps the verifier from silently accepting a key type whose signature semantics nobody here has reasoned about'), while the issuer that populates the field it reads was never narrowed to match. Two components disagree about the accepted key set, and they currently agree in practice only because every shipped client happens to generate RSA-2048. pop_test.go asserts the verifier's contract; nothing asserts that the issuer's accepted set equals it.
ranked.suggested_direction: Constrain the CSR key at the ONE place that mints the credential — agentca.SignCSR — so enroll, renew and re-key are covered by one predicate: require *rsa.PublicKey (a 2048-bit floor is optional given the runtime's own 1024-bit rule). Re-key maps the refusal into the existing uniform ErrRekeyRefused (rekey.go:194 already does); enroll/renew keep returning invalid_csr. Red it with a P-256 CSR through SignCSR and assert the verifier's accepted set (pop.go:80) and the issuer's are the SAME set rather than agreeing by luck.

ranked.title: maxLength on the re-key identifiers answers 400 where every other bad identifier answers 403 — contradicting the constraint the schema's own next line says it deliberately omits
ranked.failure_sequence:
Two finders (oracle, errors) found this independently. Verified by running the real spec through the real validator.

Input A: POST /agent/rekey/challenge {"key_fingerprint":"<201 'a'>"} → the global OpenAPI validator (router.go:210) fails maxLength: 200 and validationErrorHandler (router.go:243-252) writes 400 {"code":"validation_failed","message":"request body has an error: … Error at \"/key_fingerprint\": maximum string length is 200"} — naming the property and the bound.
Input B: the same with 65 'a' → validator returns nil, ParseRekeyIdentifier (rekeyident.go:60-64, exact-64-lowercase-hex) rejects the shape, handler returns 403 rekey_refused.
Input C: {"cert_serial":"<101 chars>"} → 400; a 100-char serial nobody holds → 200 from challenge, 403 from submit (openapi.yaml:3105, 3131).
Input D: any unknown property → 400, naming it (additionalProperties: false).

The description on the very next line (openapi.yaml:3110) states: "No length or pattern constraint here on purpose — a schema violation would answer with 400 where an unknown identifier answers 403, which is a distinction worth denying", and node_handlers.go:151-153 plus rekeyident.go:46-55 repeat the rule; docs/S13.1-decisions.md:833-835 rules it. `git log -L` shows the maxLength keyword and the sentence denying it landed in the SAME commit.

Both lenses agree the security impact is nil: the split is a pure function of the caller's own input length, invariant over all server state; the 200/100 caps sit far outside the real 64-hex identifier space so a prober never crosses them while bisecting shapes; legitimate values (64-char fingerprints, ≤32-char serials from agentca.serialString) can never be 400'd; and openapi.yaml is the public spec, so the bounds are published anyway. What remains is a documented invariant contradicted by the artifact two lines above the sentence stating it.
ranked.why_it_matters: The next reader trusts the comment over the constraint and builds on a property the code does not have — and the same file carries the endpoint's public contract ('Every failure returns the SAME refusal', openapi.yaml:1880-1882). Also worth recording: every rekey test runs BELOW the layer where the split occurs (rekey_integration_test.go and rekeyident_test.go call the service and parser directly), so the guard named in rekeyident.go's own comment as protecting uniform refusal never exercises the HTTP/validator seam where a refusal split would appear.
ranked.suggested_direction: Pick one and make the text match: either drop maxLength from cert_serial and key_fingerprint on both re-key schemas (the 64 KiB body cap already bounds the input ahead of the decoder) so every identifier problem lands on the uniform 403, or keep the caps and rewrite the description plus docs/S13.1-decisions.md:833-835 to say honestly that a coarse DoS-shaped cap far outside the 64-hex shape space is deliberate and over-length values are distinguishable. Note the fully-uniform property is unattainable for any OpenAPI-validated body (type, additionalProperties, required all produce 400s), so the honest text should scope the claim to state-dependent failures.

ranked.title: TestRekeyQueryCannotResurrect asserts substring presence, so a WHERE clause that re-keys every active node still passes the guard
ranked.failure_sequence:
The rescoped guard strips comments, lowercases, splits at the first `where`, checks the SET half contains neither "status" nor "revoked_at", then checks the WHOLE text contains the substrings `status = 'active'`, `where id = $1` and `cert_serial = $6`. It never checks how the predicates combine.

Mutation A of RekeyNode (nodes.sql:296-299):
  UPDATE nodes SET cert_serial=$2, cert_public_key=$3, cert_not_after=$4, agent_version=$5, last_seen_at=now()
  WHERE id = $1 AND cert_serial = $6 OR status = 'active' RETURNING *;
Run the guard: the setClause is byte-identical (split point unchanged, SET list untouched) so the two banned-column checks pass; the text contains `status = 'active'` (now an OR arm) so :59 passes; it contains `where id = $1` and `cert_serial = $6` so :66 passes. GREEN. AND binds tighter than OR, so the predicate is (id=$1 AND cert_serial=$6) OR status='active'.

Mutation B: `... AND (status = 'active' OR status = 'revoked')` — same four checks pass identically, and a revoked row becomes re-keyable, breaking the defence-in-depth property the guard's own failure message claims holds "even if a caller reaches this query without consulting RekeyAuthorized".

Nothing else pins the predicate: the query has no other test reference, the generated mirror (nodes.sql.go:606-611) is verbatim so make generate-check only enforces regeneration, rekey.go:202 checks only pgx.ErrNoRows with no updated.ID == node.ID assertion, and rekey_integration_test.go skips without TUNNEX_TEST_DATABASE_URL.

One lens established a bound on mutation A's blast radius: nodes_cert_serial_key is a UNIQUE index (0008_nodes.up.sql:33), so assigning one serial across multiple active rows violates it, the UPDATE errors and the transaction rolls back — so the mass rewrite is loud rather than silent with ≥2 active nodes. Mutation B is not so bounded, but the primary refusal (RekeyAuthorized) is covered behaviourally by TestRekeyNeverUnRevokes.
ranked.why_it_matters: The guard's docstring claims it proves 'a statement that never references the column cannot resurrect anything down ANY path' and that the status filter holds even without the gate. Both are false under mutations the test stays green for, on the one statement in the epic whose integrity the paper treats as structural rather than procedural — and the census law this rescope was made to satisfy is specifically about asserting the property rather than a coincidence of the text. This is the same class as backfill0055_test.go, which 'began passing on a coincidence' once RekeyNode introduced duplicate text.
ranked.suggested_direction: Assert the WHERE clause's shape rather than substrings: split on `where`, normalise whitespace and require the clause to be exactly `where id = $1 and cert_serial = $6 and status = 'active'` (or parse it and require every conjunct with no top-level OR). Cheap complement that does not depend on text at all: an integration red that seeds a revoked node, calls RekeyNode directly and asserts pgx.ErrNoRows — that fails on both mutations.

ranked.title: Migration 0061's rolling-upgrade shim protects a control-plane version that cannot exist — node_rekey_challenges is created by 0058 in the same release
ranked.failure_sequence:
Both 0058_node_rekey_challenges.up.sql (CREATE TABLE) and 0061_node_key_fingerprint.up.sql (ADD COLUMN identifier/identifier_kind) are pure additions on this branch, so they ship in one release. Verified: `git ls-tree f9b2dfd0 -- apps/api/db/migrations` ends at 0056; `git grep -c node_rekey_challenges f9b2dfd0` returns nothing; the released tags v0.3.0-rc1 and v0.3.0-rc5 have no match either. No shipped control-plane version knows the table exists.

1. 0061:47 and nodes.sql:218-224 justify writing cert_serial in CreateRekeyChallenge as: "a previous-version replica reads cert_serial, and without this it could not consume a challenge a new replica issued." That replica has no re-key code and never SELECTs, INSERTs into or reads that table. The write half (`CASE WHEN $3 = 'cert_serial' THEN $2 END`, nodes.sql:220) duplicates a value nothing will ever read; the only readers of the column in the whole tree are ConsumeRekeyChallenge's own coalesce and the 0061 down-migration.
2. ConsumeRekeyChallenge's `coalesce(identifier, cert_serial) = $2` (nodes.sql:241) is justified symmetrically as consuming a challenge the previous version issued with a NULL identifier. No such row can exist: the only writer always binds identifier unconditionally (rekey.go:53,62-68 guarantee a non-empty value), and 0061's tail backfills `SET identifier = cert_serial WHERE identifier IS NULL`. The fallback arm is reachable only from a hand-written INSERT — which is exactly and only what rekey_integration_test.go:337-339 does, labelled "a challenge as the PREVIOUS version wrote it", making the false premise look verified.
3. Carried forward: cert_serial is permanently NULLable, identifier cannot be NOT NULL, the consume predicate is wider than `identifier = $2`, and docs/S13.1-decisions.md:915-921 REGISTERS a contract migration for a release-after-next whose entire rationale is the same non-existent previous reader.

There is no runtime failure — the widened predicate matches exactly the same rows given the only writer, and the nonce PK anchors the WHERE so the extra disjunct is unreachable by any caller. The defect is that a load-bearing-looking mechanism, its justification comments, a test, and a scheduled follow-up migration all rest on a premise that is false as written.
ranked.why_it_matters: TestMigrationsAreBackwardCompatibleForOneVersion (migrationcompat_test.go:33-41) is a line-level regex over migration text with no notion of which tables the previous version touches, so it fired on a RENAME inside a table that did not exist one version ago and forced expand/contract onto it — and the resulting shim was then documented as protecting a real scenario. Anyone reading `coalesce(identifier, cert_serial)` later will reason about a NULL-identifier row no code path can produce. Note the MIGRATION SHAPE is genuinely forced by the guard and is not vacuous; only the query-level shim is dead.
ranked.suggested_direction: Cheapest honest resolution: rewrite the three justification sites — nodes.sql:218-224 (write half), nodes.sql:236-243 (read half), rekey_integration_test.go:314-329 — to say what is true (the compatibility guard is table-age-blind and fired on a table the previous version does not have; these columns are the price of not grandfathering), and re-file the registered contract migration as cleanup-of-a-guard-artifact. Alternative, which is a decide-item: add 0061 to `grandfathered` in migrationcompat_test.go with the reason 'table introduced by 0058 in the same release; no previous version reads it', fold the columns into 0058 with identifier NOT NULL, drop cert_serial, and collapse the predicate to `identifier = $2`.

roots: ROOT 1 — D3 and D10 were designed against each other on the one column both are load-bearing on. The gone-gate reads cert_not_after; a successful-but-undelivered re-key is precisely what makes cert_not_after fresh. Four independent finders (binding, replay, regression, sql) hit this; it is the single highest-confidence defect in the pass and its guard test (rekey_integration_test.go:195-198) fabricates the state that makes it pass.

ROOT 2 — attemptRekey decides its recovery inputs ONCE, before an infinite loop that never re-evaluates them and never exits on refusal. pendingWasOnDisk is sampled at entry (main.go:812), the identities slice is built at :837-849, HaveToken is never passed in at all, and the only loop exits are success and ctx-cancel. Three findings (join-token fallback unreachable, fingerprint identity never tried in-process, non-200 conflated with permanent refusal) are all instances of 'decided before the loop, never revisited'. The agent's half of the re-key protocol was never reviewed as a protocol.

ROOT 3 — the device restore is authorized by state read BEFORE the identity commit and applied AFTER it, against a candidate set keyed only on (node_id, revoked_cause='cascade') with no memory of node status, prior device status, or transport. Four findings fall out of that one shape: the post-commit revoke race, pending-devices promoted to active, OpenVPN certs left on the CRL, and out-of-pool address reclaim. The schema recorded WHY a device was revoked (0059) but not WHAT it was, and the restore statement asserts terminal values for a heterogeneous set.

ROOT 4 — node revoke authorizes on the caller's org but keys its cascades on node_id, and RevokeNode is :exec so the org mismatch is silent. One missing 'resolve the node inside the org' turns an ordinary API call into a cross-tenant destructive write whose record and effect land in different tenants. The two lint:cross-org annotations vouch for an upstream guarantee that does not exist, disarming the query-lint guard.

ROOT 5 — uniform refusal is enforced in the handler but not at the edges that answer before it. ParseRekeyIdentifier validates identifier KINDS and the fingerprint's charset but never the cert_serial VALUE, so a schema-legal NUL reaches a Postgres text bind and escapes as 500; the OpenAPI validator's maxLength answers 400 where every other bad identifier answers 403. Both break the stated contract from outside the code that implements it.

ROOT 6 — the throttle is keyed on the raw peer address, which in every shipped topology is the edge proxy, and it is registered above the access logger. One registration decision produces both a fleet-wide unauthenticated denial of the recovery path this epic exists to provide and the invisibility that makes it undiagnosable from the control plane.

ROOT 7 — guards and comments that vouch for properties the code does not have. Five instances this pass: rekeyorder_test's 'every refused request costs the same' (source-order assertion only), rekeyquery_test's substring match (accepts an OR that re-keys every active node), TestLostResponseDoesNotBrickTheGateway's hand-applied UPDATE, migration 0061's 'a previous-version replica reads cert_serial' (no such version exists), and the WALL 6 comment at rekey.go:243-252 that the callee's own comment contradicts. This is the codebase's own census law failing on the story that was supposed to satisfy it — the check could not have failed.
